transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE optional), Jamal Reyes (Acme ML Eng), Priya Singh (Acme Platform PM), Liam O'Connor (Acme CTO)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8), tradeoffs on latency and quality, and proposed pilot/benchmarks. Customer wants to understand degradation envelope on their LLM workloads and recommended rollout strategy for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Topics Covered:
- What quantization profiles we support (per-layer, per-op, INT8 symmetric/asymmetric, FP8 variants)
- Benchmarks: token latency, throughput, end-to-end p99, and quality metrics (EM/ROUGE/semantic-similarity)
- KV cache and prefix caching impacts on effective latency when using smaller batch sizes
- Failure modes and fallbacks (auto-fallback to FP16/FP32 or higher-precision shards)
- Pilot scope and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a minute. quick intros?
[00:15] Jamal (Acme): yeah hi Jamal here, ML eng, I'm running a couple of LLM features in prod, mostly retrieval augmented generation and some internal summarization.
[00:30] Priya (Acme): Priya, platform PM, i'm focused on infra cost and SLOs.
[00:35] Liam (Acme): Liam CTO - i'll jump in on security/architecture bits.
[00:40] Maya (Redwood): Maya here, i'll be doing the deep dive on Optimize and the quant profiles.
[00:50] Ethan (Redwood): great, quick agenda, show the console, run through INT8 vs FP8 tradeoffs, share benchmark results, then discuss pilot and next steps.
[01:15] Maya (Redwood): ok jumping in, first slide — uh i mean the console view, you can see we expose quant profiles at a model level. profile names are human readable, like "int8-symmetric-kv-safe" or "fp8-high-dens". those map to a set of per-layer quantization knobs.
[01:45] Jamal (Acme): when you say per-layer knobs, do you do mixed precision inside a single op? we have a few fused ops that are very sensitivity to precision.
[02:10] Maya (Redwood): yeah good question; we support mixed quant within a model, we automatically leave attention softmax and layernorm in higher precision by default, while linear mats are candidates for int8. for FP8 we often can quantize more aggressively but you might see some numerical instability on certain heads.
[03:00] Jamal (Acme): mk I see. do you have numbers on generation quality? like BLEU/ROUGE or more importantly embedding similarity for our RAG use cases.
[03:20] Maya (Redwood): we ran a few standard evals — on a 7B-ish model, int8 symmetric usually is within 0.5-1.5% on semantic-sim compared to FP16; FP8 in our tuned profile is within 0.2-1% but there are occasional outlier prompts that degrade more. the important part is we give you the distributions and per-prompt diffs in the benchmark CSV.
[04:05] Priya (Acme): so latency — are we seeing token-level latency improvements with int8 vs fp8 or vice versa?
[04:20] Maya (Redwood): latency depends on hardware and kernel support. on A100 int8 kernels can be faster for matmuls if the kernel is optimized, but FP8 often has hardware-accelerated paths on newer chips and reduces memory movement so you can see equal or better throughput. in our internal tests on T4/A10 family, int8 gave ~20-30% token latency reduction; on H100/NextGen FP8 matches or slightly betters int8 for long-context workloads.
[05:15] Liam (Acme): ok how do you handle fallback if a quantized run fails due to NaN or divergence?
[05:30] Maya (Redwood): automatic fallback is in the serving runtime: near-detect of numeric instability will roll the request to a compatible higher precision shard (fp16). also we surface alerts in the console and you can set rollout policies to gradually ramp quant profiles per customer.
[06:10] Jamal (Acme): any impact on KV cache size? if we store kv in int8 does that reduce memory and improve throughput?
[06:30] Maya (Redwood): yes kv cache compresses with quantization: int8 reduces memory on the kv cache noticeably which helps with larger batch sizes; however you pay a small CPU decompress/rehydrate cost at read which can add microseconds. we show this in the per-token breakdown.
[07:00] Ethan (Redwood): pulling up the benchmark sheet — quick note: these are synthetic but we've also run customer-like workloads. Maya, can you call out the p50/p95/p99 numbers?
[07:15] Maya (Redwood): sure, for a 7B model with 512 tokens context and batch size 1, int8 profile p50 token latency ~18ms, p95 ~34ms, p99 ~72ms; FP8 tuned profile p50 ~20ms, p95 ~30ms, p99 ~65ms. so FP8 slightly better at the tail in that run but your mileage varies.
[08:00] Jamal (Acme): interesting, that p99 difference is key for our SLOs. how stable are those numbers across longer sequences?
[08:20] Maya (Redwood): as sequence length grows, FP8's memory improvements help keep p99 stable because you avoid memory thrashing. int8 can still be beneficial at short sequences. this is why we suggested evaluating both on your real prompts.
[09:00] Priya (Acme): security/compliance question — are quantized artifacts stored differently? we need to ensure any model artifacts in Dedicated/on-prem remain under our control and encrypted.
[09:20] Ethan (Redwood): yes for Dedicated and Private deployments you control KMS keys and artifacts are stored encrypted; quant profiles are metadata and the artifacts we generate for serving can be confined to the customer's VPC, and audit logs include quant profile changes.
[09:50] Liam (Acme): do you support S3-like object retention policies or immutability for audit?
[10:05] Ethan (Redwood): we integrate with customer object stores for Private; for Hosted we can provide retention settings and exportable audit logs. we'll send the SOC2/ISO docs.
[10:30] Maya (Redwood): back to quality — i want to call out a couple of typical failure cases: very low-temperature deterministic decoding sometimes surfaces quantization artifacts; also certain tokenizers with large vocab tails can amplify errors. we recommend running a prompt-differential test set — which you already offered to provide.
[11:15] Jamal (Acme): yeah we'll share 3 prompt sets, some RAG prompts and internal summarization.
[11:30] Maya (Redwood): perfect. demo time — i'll flip to the console, showing Optimize -> Profiles. you can create a new profile, select base model, choose int8 symmetric or asymmetric, enable bias correction, and toggle per-op exclusions.
[12:00] (screen share noise)
[12:30] Maya (Redwood): creating profile now — name it "acme-int8-safe". selecting exclude for layernorm. we'll run the benchmark harness in the cloud, and you can opt to run it on Dedicated or Hosted.
[13:00] Priya (Acme): what about cost delta — do we have per-token cost savings estimates?
[13:15] Ethan (Redwood): empirically we've seen 20-45% cost reductions depending on profile and workload; int8 typically sits at the higher end for short contexts, FP8 for long contexts often wins because you fit more requests per GPU. we'll include a modeled cost sheet.
[14:00] Jamal (Acme): for our compliance we need to log model version + quant profile used per request. is that available in the request trace?
[14:20] Maya (Redwood): yes trace includes model version, quant profile, kernel variant, and hardware id. Console shows these in the per-request trace and you can stream to your SIEM.
[15:00] (short cross talk)
[15:30] Priya (Acme): latency SLO wise if we roll a quant profile to 100% what rollback options exist?
[15:45] Maya (Redwood): rollouts support canary and automatic rollback policies. you can set an error/latency threshold; if exceeded the system will revert to the previous profile. also we support traffic splitting to compare quality metrics side-by-side.
[16:30] Ethan (Redwood): show a live side-by-side A/B of outputs?
[16:40] Maya (Redwood): yes — here is a snapshot: fp16 vs int8 output similarity is 98.7% on our sample, fp8 vs fp16 99.1%. note the distributions show a handful of prompts with 70-80% similarity; you can flag those for manual review.
[17:30] Jamal (Acme): can we ship a hybrid where short latency critical routes use int8 and long batch jobs use fp8?
[17:45] Maya (Redwood): absolutely, routing policies support per-route quant profiles. you can also route by header, user tier, or latency budget.
[18:15] Liam (Acme): what about on-prem latency characteristics? we plan an air-gapped evaluation on our DGX cluster, any caveats?
[18:35] Maya (Redwood): main caveat is kernel support on your drivers; we'll provide a compatibility matrix. some FP8 fast paths require recent drivers and compiler toolchain; we'll help collect the env details for your infra team.
[19:20] Ethan (Redwood): also note Dedicated gives you reserved capacity which helps with p99 stability compared to bursty hosted tiers.
[19:40] Priya (Acme): good to know.
[20:00] (screen share pauses for file upload)
[21:00] Maya (Redwood): uploading the benchmark CSV to the shared drive now — link posted in the chat: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/acme-int8-fp8-2025-12-03.csv (note: link is placeholder in transcript).
[21:30] Jamal (Acme): quick question on eval metrics: you mentioned semantic-sim, do you use cosine on embeddings or LLM-scored similarity?
[21:45] Maya (Redwood): both — we compute embedding cosine and also run a LLM-consistency scorer for generative outputs. we surface both and an aggregate quality delta.
[22:30] Priya (Acme): how much effort is required to run the POC? headcount/time?
[22:45] Ethan (Redwood): pilot typically runs 2-4 weeks: Redwood SE runs initial benchmarks and helps tune quant profiles (1-2 weeks), then a customer-run production-like test for 1-2 weeks. required customer time is usually an engineer to validate outputs and a platform person to coordinate infra.
[23:30] Jamal (Acme): ok that fits our timeline, we want results before end of Jan.
[23:45] Maya (Redwood): we can schedule a POC scoping call next week to lock in datasets and infra.
[24:15] (discussion on contractual/compliance asks)
[27:00] Ethan (Redwood): quick recap of asks: Maya to share CSV and runbook; Ethan to share pricing; Jamal to share prompts; schedule POC scoping.
[27:30] Priya (Acme): can you include a section on rollback SLAs?
[27:45] Ethan (Redwood): yes we'll add rollback SLOs to the pilot doc.
[28:00] (some background noise)
[30:00] Liam (Acme): one last technical — quantization and explainability: will our logs be adequate for audits if regulators ask about why model produced something?
[30:20] Maya (Redwood): yes we persist request traces, model provenance, quant profile versions, and a per-token cost/latency breakdown; you can export these as CSVs for audit.
[31:00] Jamal (Acme): do you support deterministic seeds for eval? we need repeatability for regression tests.
[31:20] Maya (Redwood): deterministic runs are supported in the benchmark harness; note that some quantized kernels have non-deterministic reductions on certain hardware — we'll flag those.
[32:00] Ethan (Redwood): okay i'm going to drop the shared checklist in the chat: pilot intake form, infra checklist, and security questionnaire.
[32:20] (chat link posted)
[33:00] Priya (Acme): thanks; any initial blockers?
[33:10] Jamal (Acme): just driver/compatibility on our on-prem cluster — we'll validate and report back.
[33:30] Maya (Redwood): we'll send the compatibility matrix and a quick script to collect driver info.
[34:00] (wrap up)
[34:30] Ethan (Redwood): great, thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar for POC scoping.
[34:45] Jamal (Acme): thanks all.
[35:00] (meeting ends)
